# Before you start {#sec-start .unnumbered}

This page covers three things:

1. the statistics and R that the book assumes, with a short refresher for
   each;
2. setting up your computer, including the files to download;
3. how the book is laid out.

If you're comfortable with the refreshers, skim them and go straight to
setting up.

## What the book assumes {#sec-assumed}

You don't need to know anything about survival analysis or propensity
scores. You *do* need some basic statistics. Open any refresher below that
you're unsure about.

| Idea | Where it's used |
|---|---|
| Means, proportions and standard deviations | Throughout, especially Chapter 5 (SMDs) |
| Confidence intervals | Throughout |
| p-values and hypothesis tests | Chapters 2–7 |
| Regression: an outcome explained by several predictors | Chapters 3–7 |
| Odds, odds ratios and logistic regression | Chapter 5 |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Refresher: standard deviation
The **standard deviation (SD)** measures how spread out values are around
their mean. If ages in a group have mean 65 and SD 10, most people are
roughly between 55 and 75. In Chapter 5, differences between groups are
measured *in units of SD* (the standardised mean difference), so that age
in years and BMI in kg/m² can be compared on the same scale.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Refresher: confidence intervals
A **95% confidence interval (CI)** gives a range of plausible values for
the true quantity, based on the data. "Median survival 310 days (95% CI
285 to 363)" means the data are consistent with a true median anywhere in
roughly that range. Wider intervals mean less certainty, usually because
of less data.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Refresher: p-values and hypothesis tests
A test starts from a **null hypothesis**, usually "no difference". The
**p-value** is the probability of getting data at least as extreme as
yours *if the null hypothesis were true*. A small p-value (conventionally
< 0.05) is evidence against the null.

Three things to remember:

- A p-value is **not** the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
- A small p-value doesn't mean the difference is large or important.
  Always look at the size of the effect and its CI.
- Each test at the 5% level has a 5% chance of a false positive, so
  running many tests produces false positives. That's why multiple
  comparisons are adjusted (Chapter 2).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Refresher: regression and "adjusting for" variables
A **regression model** relates an outcome to several predictors at once.
Each predictor's coefficient describes its effect **holding the other
predictors fixed**. That's what "adjusted for age and sex" means: the
comparison is between people of the same age and sex. Linear regression
does this for a continuous outcome. The Cox model (Chapter 3) does it for
survival.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Refresher: odds, odds ratios and logistic regression
If the probability of an event is $p$, the **odds** are $p / (1 - p)$.

| Probability | Odds | Log-odds (logit) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 1 | 0 |
| 0.8 | 4 | 1.39 |
| 0.2 | 0.25 | −1.39 |

An **odds ratio (OR)** compares the odds in two groups. OR = 2 means the
odds are doubled. **Logistic regression** models a yes/no outcome. Its
coefficients are log odds ratios, and `exp()` turns them into odds ratios.
The **log-odds** (or *logit*) scale stretches probabilities near 0 and 1
out evenly, which is why Chapter 5 measures distances between propensity
scores on that scale.
:::

## The R you need {#sec-r-basics}

You should be able to run code in RStudio (or Positron), create objects
with `<-`, and install and load packages. The book also uses a few other
features again and again. Here they are in one place.

**Data frames and columns.** A dataset is a *data frame*: one row per
patient, one column per variable. `df$age` is the `age` column, and
`head(df)` shows the first rows.

**Factors.** A *factor* is a categorical variable with fixed *levels*, e.g.
`sex` with levels `"Male"` and `"Female"`. In models, the **first level is
the reference group** that the other levels are compared with.

**Formulas.** Almost every modelling function uses a formula,
`outcome ~ predictors`:

```r
glm(treated ~ age + diabetes, data = cohort, family = binomial)  # treated explained by age and diabetes
coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung)               # survival explained by sex and age
survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = lung)                     # ~ 1 means "no groups"
```

In survival models the outcome is `Surv(time, status)`, which combines
follow-up time and whether the event happened (Chapter 1).

**The pipe, `|>`.** Read it as "and then". These two lines do the same
thing:

```r
summary(filter(lung, age > 60))
lung |> filter(age > 60) |> summary()
```

**A few dplyr functions.** These come from the dplyr package:

- `mutate()` creates or changes a column;
- `filter()` keeps the rows that meet a condition;
- `select()` keeps chosen columns;
- `group_by()` + `summarise()` calculates summaries for each group.

**Getting help.** Type `?coxph` (or any function name) in the console.

## Setting up your computer {#sec-setup}

::: {.callout-tip}
## You can start without installing anything
The exercises in Chapters 1–7 and 9–11 run R **inside the web page** (see
@sec-live-exercises), so you can work through the whole book in your
browser. Set up R on your own computer when you want to run the code
yourself, use the Shiny apps in Chapter 8, or analyse your own data.
:::

### 1. Install R, RStudio and the packages

Install [R](https://cran.r-project.org) (version 4.2 or later) and
[RStudio Desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/). Then run
this once in the RStudio console:

```r
install.packages(c(
  "survival",   # survival data, Kaplan-Meier, log-rank test, Cox models
  "ggsurvfit",  # Kaplan-Meier plots
  "survminer",  # pairwise log-rank tests
  "MatchIt",    # propensity score matching
  "cobalt",     # checking covariate balance
  "broom",      # tidy tables of model results
  "dplyr", "ggplot2", "tidyr",
  "shiny"       # only needed for the apps in Chapter 8
))

# Only needed for the Going further chapters (9-11)
install.packages(c("WeightIt", "survRM2", "mice", "MatchThem"))
```

### 2. Make a project folder

In RStudio, choose **File ▸ New Project ▸ New Directory ▸ New Project**,
and call it something like `survival-course`. RStudio will look in this
folder for any files you load. Save everything for this course there.

### 3. Download the course files

Save these files into your project folder:

| File | What it is | Used in |
|---|---|---|
| [simulate_cohort.R](R/simulate_cohort.R){download="simulate_cohort.R"} | Function that creates the simulated cohort | Chapters 5–7 |
| [cohort.csv](data/cohort.csv){download="cohort.csv"} | The same simulated cohort, as a spreadsheet file | Chapters 5–7 (alternative to the script) |
| [pairwise_logrank.R](R/pairwise_logrank.R){download="pairwise_logrank.R"} | Optional helper showing how pairwise log-rank tests work | Chapter 2 (optional) |
| [survival-explorer.R](apps/survival-explorer/app.R){download="survival-explorer.R"} | Shiny app: KM curves and Cox models on real data | Chapter 8 |
| [psm-explorer.R](apps/psm-explorer/app.R){download="psm-explorer.R"} | Shiny app: matching vs weighting vs adjustment | Chapter 8 |

The other datasets (`lung`, `veteran`, `mgus2`, `jasa` and `heart`) come
with the survival package, so you don't need to download them.

### 4. Check that everything works

Run this in the console, from inside your project:

```r
library(survival)
library(ggsurvfit)
library(survminer)
library(MatchIt)
library(cobalt)

source("simulate_cohort.R")       # loads the simulate_cohort() function
cohort <- simulate_cohort()
nrow(cohort)                      # should print 2000
```

If you get *"cannot open file 'simulate_cohort.R'"*, the file isn't in your
project folder. Check where it was downloaded, and move it.

## How the book is laid out {#sec-layout}

Each chapter mixes reading, R code, interactive apps and practice. The
boxes always mean the same thing:

| Box | What it's for |
|---|---|
| **In this chapter** / **Summary** | The question each chapter answers, and later the key points and the answer. A **Warm-up** with two recall questions comes first from Chapter 2 on |
| **How to read this output** | Points out the few numbers that matter in a block of R output |
| **Things to try** / **Answers** | Guided activities for an app: predict first, then check the collapsed answers |
| **Practice**, **Exercise** and **Quick quiz** | Live R code boxes in the page with hints and automatic checking (R loads in your browser the first time, 10–30 seconds), then quiz questions with instant feedback |
| **Going further (optional)** | Extra depth, collapsed. **Skip these on a first read.** The main text never depends on them. Many end with a link to the fuller treatment in the Going further part |
| **You need this chapter if…** | At the start of each chapter in the *Going further* part (Chapters 9–11), which are for when your own analysis needs them. It says when the chapter applies to you, and which core chapters it builds on |

If you meet a term you don't recognise, look it up in the
[Glossary](a2-glossary.qmd).

::: {.callout-tip}
## A suggested way to work
On your first pass, read the main text, use the apps, and do the quizzes
and exercises. Skip the "Going further" boxes. Come back to them once the
main ideas feel familiar, or when you need one for your own analysis.
:::
